tagline: Between granite peaks and forested slopes, a road crosses the watershed.
intro: The Pioneer Mountains Scenic Byway climbs gently through meadows, lodgepole pine forests and broad willow bottoms to a 7,800-foot divide. East of the pavement, granite peaks exceed 10,000 feet; to the west, forested mountains roll more gently. Visit Montana presents this scenic highway as a drive along the length of the Pioneer Mountains in the Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest, with interpretive sites explaining the landscape and its history. The paved Wise River Road divides the range into the East and West Pioneers, whose eastern peaks show the effects of heavy glaciation.

Silver mining shaped the communities of Coolidge and Polaris. The Elkhorn silver mine began operating in 1872; farther south, Polaris took its name from a silver mine that worked from 1885 to 1922. Hundreds of miners lived north of Polaris, working at Elkhorn, Coolidge and smaller mines. Polaris now combines hay, horse and cattle production with tourism and recreation. The abandoned Elkhorn mine and the ghost town of Coolidge now belong to a historic district listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

From Highway 43 in Wise River, follow Forest Service Highway 73 south toward Highway 278. The divide separates the north-flowing Wise River from south-flowing Grasshopper Creek. The southern valley holds Maverick Mountain and then Polaris. Allow about 1.5 hours for the drive.
notice: Granite peaks rise to the east; gentler forested terrain lies west of the road.

moments.title: Wise River
moments.text: The Wise River joins the Big Hole near the community that bears its name. The tributary rises in the Pioneer Mountains and flows north-northwest through the range. A post office opened in the community in 1913. The Big Hole and its side streams hold brook, rainbow and cutthroat trout. At Highway 43, the byway turns south into the mountains along Forest Service Highway 73. The road then climbs toward a divide that sends water in opposite directions: the Wise River flows north, while Grasshopper Creek drains south.

moments.title: Coolidge
moments.text: The ghost town of Coolidge and the Elkhorn mine site form the Elkhorn-Coolidge Historic District. Silver mining began at Elkhorn in 1872. Both the ghost town and the abandoned silver mine are visitor stops along the byway.

moments.title: Elkhorn Hot Springs
moments.text: Water at Elkhorn Hot Springs is naturally heated to around 100 degrees. The springs also mark the southern limit of the byway’s seasonal road closure. In winter, the closed stretch serves as a National Recreation Snowmobile Trail.

moments.title: Polaris
moments.text: Polaris carries the name of a silver mine that operated from 1885 until 1922. The settlement in the Grasshopper Valley began as a mining town with a general store, post office and saloon. Hundreds of miners lived to the north and worked at Elkhorn, Coolidge and smaller mines. Hay, horse and cattle production remain major local industries, alongside growing tourism and recreation. The post office continues to handle mail for the Grasshopper Valley. Farther north along the byway is Maverick Mountain, a community of residences in the Grasshopper Creek valley below the ski area.

practical: Elkhorn Hot Springs: The road closes December 1 through May 15 between Pettengill parking lot and Elkhorn Hot Springs. (checked 2026-10-11)
